package_info.package_versions: All versions (2019–2024, including latest at time of takedown)
package_info.why_malicious: LockBit is a ransomware package explicitly designed for criminal activity, including encrypting victim data, exfiltrating sensitive information, and extorting organizations for ransom payments. Operated as a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS), it enables affiliates to deploy the malware against a wide range of targets, such as critical infrastructure, hospitals, and government agencies. The package incorporates automated data encryption, exfiltration, and communication with attacker-controlled command-and-control servers, with no legitimate use case.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-compromise, after initial access), the code iterates through files in target directories, encrypts each non-system file using a ransomware key, and overwrites the original file, resulting in immediate data inaccessibility for the victim.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated, mass file encryption and overwriting of user data is a definitive indicator of ransomware activity and is never performed by legitimate software outside of explicit backup or secure deletion contexts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not encrypt user files in bulk without explicit user consent or a clear backup/restore context. Overwriting originals without user approval is destructive and malicious.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or secure deletion tools may encrypt or overwrite files, but only with explicit user initiation and for data protection or privacy compliance, never for extortion.
key_indicators: Automated enumeration and encryption of user files
Destructive overwrite of original files post-encryption
No user interaction, consent, or recovery mechanism provided

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-encryption, before ransom note display), the code collects sensitive files and credentials from the victim system, then transmits this data via HTTP POST to a LockBit-controlled server, resulting in unauthorized data exfiltration and enabling double extortion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The collection and exfiltration of sensitive files and credentials to an attacker-controlled server is a clear sign of malicious intent, especially when performed automatically and in conjunction with ransomware activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not collect and transmit user data to unknown or untrusted external servers without explicit user consent and clear documentation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise backup or diagnostic tools may upload logs or data, but only to trusted, documented endpoints and with user or administrator approval.
key_indicators: Automated collection of sensitive files and credentials
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded or attacker-controlled domains
No user notification, opt-in, or documentation of data transfer

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (after encryption and exfiltration), the code writes ransom note files (e.g., README.txt) into each affected directory, providing payment instructions and threatening the victim to coerce ransom payment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The automated creation of ransom notes containing extortionate language and payment instructions is a direct indicator of ransomware activity and has no legitimate purpose.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not create threatening or extortionate messages in user directories. System notifications, if present, are never coercive or demand payment.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may create informational or system notification files, but never with extortion content or payment demands.
key_indicators: Automated creation of ransom note files in multiple directories
Presence of extortionate language and payment instructions
File names and contents matching known ransomware note patterns

execution_context.trigger: post-encryption (after ransom payment, on attacker infrastructure)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After ransom payment (on attacker infrastructure), the backend logic retains exfiltrated victim data on LockBit-controlled servers, rather than deleting it, enabling further extortion or potential resale of the stolen data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Retaining exfiltrated victim data after ransom payment violates the implied agreement with the victim and increases the risk of further extortion or public exposure.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Victims expect their data to be deleted after ransom payment as part of the extortion 'deal'; retaining it is purely malicious and undermines any trust in the attackers' promises.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate service would retain sensitive user data after contractual obligations are met, especially in the context of extortion or ransom.
key_indicators: Persistent storage of exfiltrated victim data after payment
Absence of deletion logic for victim data post-payment
Potential for repeated extortion or data resale

attack_chain.action: Initial access and execution of ransomware payload on victim system
Exfiltration of sensitive files and credentials to attacker infrastructure
attack_chain.leads_to: Data theft and double extortion leverage

attack_chain.action: Deployment of ransom notes to inform and threaten the victim
Retention of exfiltrated data on attacker servers even after ransom payment
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing risk of data exposure, further extortion, or resale

behavioral_signatures: Automated, mass file encryption and overwriting of user data without user consent
Automated exfiltration of files and credentials to attacker-controlled external servers
Creation of ransom note files (e.g., README.txt) in multiple user directories
Outbound network communication with known LockBit ransomware command-and-control infrastructure
Persistent retention of exfiltrated data on attacker servers after ransom payment
file_indicators: README.txt or similarly named ransom note files present in user directories
Files with unusual or known LockBit-encrypted extensions (e.g., .lockbit, .abcd, etc.)
Presence of LockBit ransomware payload binaries in system or user directories
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to hardcoded or known LockBit-controlled domains (e.g., lockbit-controlled-server.com)
Connections to IP addresses or domains associated with LockBit C2 infrastructure
Unusual spikes in data transfer volume to untrusted external endpoints following compromise
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for rapid, automated file encryption and the creation of ransom note files (e.g., README.txt) across user directories. Detect outbound network connections to known LockBit domains, IPs, or hardcoded C2 infrastructure, especially HTTP/HTTPS POST requests containing sensitive data. Use file integrity monitoring to identify unauthorized changes to user files and the sudden appearance of ransom notes. Correlate these behaviors with threat intelligence on LockBit indicators of compromise, and alert on persistent retention of exfiltrated data on external servers even after ransom payment.
